- Look at the guards. Is there a defensive tackle on a guard's *outside* shoulder? That is the
  3-technique, and his side of the line is where the defense has put its quickness. Is there one big man
  right over the center? That is a 0 nose, likely playing both A gaps.
- Look at the ends. Shaded on the tackle (a 5)? Way out wide, past where a tight end would be (a wide-9)?
  Standing up outside the tight end (a 9)? Wider ends mean more pass rush and bigger run lanes inside them.

**At the snap: the first step.**

- Does the lineman's first step go *into a gap*, upfield (one-gap), or *into the blocker*, with his hands,
  standing him up (two-gap)?
- Does the whole line step sideways together at the snap? That is a slant; look for the linebackers to shift
  the other way. One man darting into the next gap while the rest go straight is an angle.

**After the play: where did the run go?**

- Which way did the run go relative to the 3-technique: at him, or away? Did he get into the backfield, get
  double-teamed, or get trapped?
- Did the run get outside the edge? If it did, ask who had the edge on that side and whether he got hooked.
  On a bootleg or scramble, ask who had contain.

For your prediction log ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
before each early-down snap, note which side the 3-technique is on. After the play, note whether the run went
toward him or away from him. A few quarters of that will tell you something about both coordinators.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. One-gap or two-gap?** Two fronts against the same one-tight-end offense, before the snap. For each
one, guess how its linemen will play (attack a gap, or control a blocker and read), what kind of bodies you
expect to see, and which defenders you expect to be *free* to run to the ball.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: two fronts against the same offense. Front A: three linemen head-up (a 0 on the center and a 4 on each tackle), outside linebackers (B) on the edges, two inside linebackers. Front B: four linemen shaded (5, 1, 3, 9) and three linebackers."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
fronts = [("Front A", front([("LE", "4", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4", 1)],
                             lbs=[("MIKE", 4.6, -1.8, "M"), ("WILL", 4.6, 1.8, "W")],
                             others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -5.6, "B"), ("ROLB", 1.0, 6.5, "B")])),
          ("Front B", front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
                             lbs=[("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.0, "M"), ("SAM", 4.3, 4.4, "S")]))]
for ax, (ttl, dfn) in zip(axes, fronts):
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.0, 0, "R")], dfn, los=40,
             to_go=10)
    draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-7.6, 8.6), window=(-7.4, 6.4), title=False)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Front A looks built to two-gap; Front B looks built to one-gap.** The clue is the alignments. Every lineman in
Front A is *head-up* on a blocker (0, 4, 4), and a head-up alignment doesn't put a defender in either gap, so the
natural job is to control the man and take whichever side the ball goes: the nose both A gaps, each end the B and
C gaps on his side. Expect big bodies: a nose well over 320 pounds, long ends near 300. The free players are the
two inside linebackers, who have no gap to rush to at the snap and can run to the ball, as long as the three big
men keep all five offensive linemen busy.

Every lineman in Front B is *shaded*, sitting in a gap (5 in the C, 1 in the A, 3 in the B, 9 in the D), which is
what a one-gap front looks like: each attacks the gap he is in and the three linebackers take the three that are
left (left B, right A, right C). Expect a quick 3-technique, lighter ends and more penetration. Nobody in Front B
is "free"; everybody has a gap, and the defense's bet is that each of them wins his.

**The catch:** alignment is a strong hint, not a guarantee. Wade Phillips ran a one-gap defense out of 3-4 looks for
decades, and many 4-3 teams ask a 1-technique to play both A gaps. Confirm it with the first step after the snap:
into the gap, or into the man.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. The slant meets the run.** First-and-10. The offense runs inside zone to the right. At the snap, the
defense's four linemen all slant to the right, toward the tight end, and the picture below is the first
half-second. Where is the run most likely to go now, and which defender does the defense need to be right?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: the first half-second. The offense's line steps right for inside zone and the back aims at the right guard's outside hip; the defense's linemen (orange arrows; drawn a little deeper than real) all slant hard to the right at the snap, the end outside the tight end widening. The linebackers have not moved yet."
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.0, "M"), ("SAM", 4.4, 4.6, "S")])
dfn = [q.moved(d=2.1) if q.d == 1.0 else q for q in dfn]    # linemen drawn a little deep so the slant shows
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 2: inside zone right meets a slant right")
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(0.3, 0.7)])
for k, end in [("LE", (0.8, -2.45)), ("L1", (0.8, 0.85)), ("R3", (0.8, 4.0)), ("RE", (0.7, 7.0))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.6, 1.6), "run", via=[(-6.2, 0.6)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, -0.4), "path", speed=3.0)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.5, lateral=(-8.6, 10.0), window=(-8.6, 7.4))
say(f, p, 6.3, 0.0, "linebackers: not yet moved", fontsize=6.9)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely back to the left, on the cutback.** The slant went the same way as the play, so the play side is
crowded: each defensive lineman has stepped across the face of a blocker into the next gap toward the tight end,
and the gaps the back was aiming at (the right A and B) now have defenders arriving in them. Zone blocking
absorbs some of that (each lineman simply blocks whoever came into his area), but the back reads a crowded play
side and does what inside zone teaches him: he *bends* it back toward the gaps the slant just emptied, the left A
and B.

**The defender who has to be right is the Will** (the backside linebacker). On a slant the linebackers replace the
gaps the line left, and the backside gaps are the Will's. If he remembered the call and filled, the back cuts back
into him for a short gain, and the slant won. If he flowed right with everything else, the cutback lane is empty and
the next defender is a safety. That is the bet every slant makes: it is great when it guesses the direction, and the
linebackers have to clean up when it doesn't.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. Who has contain?** Third-and-7. The offense is in the shotgun with an empty-looking
backfield and a quarterback who likes to run. The defense rushes four: a wide-9 on the right, a 5 on the left, and
two tackles inside. Which rushers have contain, how should they rush, and where is the quarterback most likely to
escape if somebody gets it wrong?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: third-and-7, shotgun, a mobile quarterback. The defense rushes four (orange arrows show the first steps; linemen drawn a little deeper than real): the wide-9 on the right, the 5 on the left, a 3 and a 1 inside. Everyone else drops into coverage (not shown)."
off = line("full") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.5, "R")]
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1)]) + [D("RE", "DL", 1.0, T("wide9") - 1.0, "w9")]
dfn = [q.moved(d=1.9) for q in dfn]                         # drawn a little deep so the first steps show
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7, title="Drill 3: four rushers, one mobile quarterback")
for k, end in [("LE", (-1.2, -5.2)), ("L1", (0.5, -0.85)), ("R3", (0.5, 2.5)), ("RE", (-1.4, 6.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "path", speed=3.0)
for k in OL_KEYS:
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-9.0, 10.0), window=(-8.6, 8.4))
say(f, p, -7.4, 3.6, "a quarterback\nwho likes to run", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The two ends have contain: the 5 on the left and the wide-9 on the right.** Their rule is to rush *outside* the
tackles but not *past* the quarterback's depth. If either one runs a wide arc around the tackle and keeps going,
he ends up behind the quarterback, and the space between him and the defensive tackle next to him becomes a
running lane. A mobile quarterback steps up into the pocket and out through that lane, usually for a first down
on third-and-7.

**The wide-9 is the likeliest to get it wrong**, because his whole alignment is built for a long, fast arc to the
quarterback. Against a runner he has to flatten his rush earlier and stay level with the quarterback. The two
inside rushers have the opposite job: push the middle of the pocket back into the quarterback so he can't step up.
A four-man rush against a mobile quarterback is a box: two sides that must hold, and a front that must squeeze.
When one side bursts, look for the quarterback there. [The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) has the
rest of this, including the stunts that trade one rusher's lane for another's.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Alignment is a job description.** The nose (0 or 1) anchors against double teams and wants mass; the
  3-technique gets a one-on-one with a guard and wants quickness; the 4i and 5 want length to control a tackle; the
  9 and the wide-9 want speed, and the wider the end, the more pass rush and the bigger the run lane inside him.
- **One-gap attacks.** Each lineman owns one gap and attacks it, aiming for penetration. It wins with quickness,
  creates sacks and tackles for loss, and turns the linemen loose, but a wrong guess leaves an empty gap, and traps,
  draws and screens are built to punish it.
- **Two-gap controls.** A head-up lineman strikes the blocker, locks out, reads (the blocker's head tells him where
  the ball is going) and sheds to the ball's side. One man covering two gaps frees the linebackers, at the cost of
  rare bodies, little pass rush, and a stat sheet that hides his value.
- **Fight pressure with pressure.** Against a down block, the man blocked fights back outward and the man left alone
  squeezes and looks for the puller; against a reach, step with the blocker and keep the outside arm free; against a
  double team, give no ground and keep both blockers.
- **The edge is everybody's boundary.** Setting the edge turns runs back inside; contain keeps the quarterback and
  the misdirection plays from getting outside. Both ask an aggressive player for patience.
- **Movement changes the picture after the snap.** Slants shift the whole line a gap; angles move one man while he
  keeps attacking. Both beat pre-snap blocking assignments and both are bets on direction that the linebackers have
  to back up.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**Penetration, measured.** Tracking data turns this chapter's distinction into a number. A one-gap penetrator is
*behind* the line of scrimmage a second after the snap; a two-gapper is *at* it. In the two simulated plays above,
here is how far each ringed defender is past the line (negative numbers mean he is in the offense's backfield),
computed from their Big Data Bowl-format tracking frames exactly as you would from real data:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (depth past the line of scrimmage, from tracking frames)"
def depth_table(plays, times=(0.3, 0.6, 1.0)):
    rows = []
    for name, play, key in plays:
        trk = play.to_tracking()
        los = trk.loc[(trk["displayName"] == "football") & (trk["time"] == 0.0), "x"].iloc[0]
        me = trk[trk["displayName"] == key].set_index("time")
        rows.append({"defender": name, **{f"+{t:.1f} s": round(float(me.loc[round(t, 1), "x"] - los), 1)
                                          for t in times}})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("defender")


depth_table([("one-gap 3-technique (simulated)", P_ONE, "R3"),
             ("two-gap nose (simulated)", P_TWO_R, "NT")]).reset_index()
```

The same calculation on real frames is a few lines with `gridiron.bdb`. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season,
weeks 1–9) has every player's location ten times a second, and its players file has his position label, so you can find each interior
defensive lineman on each run and measure how deep he is at one second. Aggregated by player, it separates the
penetrators from the anchors. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this cell is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position", "displayName"]]
runs = plays[plays["isDropback"] == False]                       # not a dropback: designed runs (plus kneels)
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
if "position" not in trk:                                        # 2025 tracking has no position column:
    trk = trk.merge(players[["nflId", "position"]], on="nflId", how="left")   # take it from players.csv

out = []
for g, pl in runs[["gameId", "playId"]].itertuples(index=False):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl, label="position")
    los = one.loc[(one["side"] == "ball") & (one["time"] == 0.0), "x"].iloc[0]
    at1 = one[(one["time"].round(1) == 1.0) & one["position"].isin(["DT", "NT"])]
    out += [{"nflId": r.nflId, "depth": r.x - los} for r in at1.itertuples()]

depth = (pd.DataFrame(out).merge(players, on="nflId")
         .groupby("displayName")["depth"].agg(["mean", "count"]).query("count >= 50").sort_values("mean"))
depth.head(10)    # the deepest penetrators (most negative = furthest into the backfield)
```
:::
